keyVerseText: Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.
rootMeaning: The word ὅριον (hórion) is derived as a neuter form from the primary Greek term ὅρος (hóros), which means a bound or limit. This etymology highlights that ὅριον fundamentally denotes a boundary or border, emphasizing a physical or conceptual limit that defines space or territory. Unlike the English word 'border,' which can be abstract or political, the root sense of ὅριον carries a tangible sense of a marked or recognized dividing line or edge.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ὅριον is used primarily to denote physical boundaries such as coasts, borders, or frontiers, appearing eleven times in the New Testament. Its frequent translation as 'the coasts' or 'coasts' (in seven of the eleven occurrences) shows a consistent connection to geographic limits, often describing the edges of a region or territory. This usage underscores the word's role in marking the extent of a place, whether literal land boundaries or figurative limits, reflecting a stable semantic range focused on spatial demarcation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὅριον as a boundary or limit enriches our grasp of biblical geography and God's sovereign ordering of creation. Boundaries signify God's design in structuring the world, separating peoples and places according to His divine purpose. The concept also points to spiritual truths about limits—God sets boundaries for human behavior and for the unfolding of His redemptive plan. Recognizing these boundaries invites believers to trust in God's control over history and geography, affirming that nothing lies outside His ordained limits. This reinforces the Christian hope that God's kingdom, though it may cross earthly borders, ultimately respects and transcends all human boundaries.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 2:16, the term ὅριον is translated as 'coasts,' describing the extent of Herod's cruel decree to kill all male children in Bethlehem and its surrounding areas. The use of ὅριον here conveys not just the city itself but the full territorial boundary under Herod's influence, emphasizing the comprehensive scope of his wrath. This highlights the tragic reality of evil reaching to the very edges of God's people, yet also sets the stage for God's protective providence extending beyond these borders through the Messiah.
